title: Act IV, Scene III
focus: testing loyalty and the cost of grief

teacherSummary.text: In England, Malcolm tests Macduff by claiming to be lustful, greedy and without any of the 'king-becoming graces.' When Macduff despairs ('O Scotland, Scotland!'), Malcolm reveals it was a test and that old Siward with ten thousand men is ready. A Doctor describes King Edward healing the sick by touch. Ross arrives and, after hesitating, tells Macduff his wife and children have been slaughtered. Macduff asks 'All my pretty ones?' and, told to 'dispute it like a man,' answers 'I shall do so; but I must also feel it as a man.' He vows to face Macbeth.

context.history: The 'king's evil' (scrofula) was believed to be cured by a monarch's touch; James I continued the ceremony. The scene contrasts a healing king with a destroying one.

significance: The long test scene defines good kingship, and Macduff's grief redefines manhood: feeling is not weakness. This answers Lady Macbeth's use of manhood in I.vii.

words.sentence:
But I shall crave your pardon;
That which you are my thoughts cannot transpose:
Angels are bright still, though the brightest fell:
Though all things foul would wear the brows of grace,
Yet grace must still look so.

But fear not yet
To take upon you what is yours: you may
Convey your pleasures in a spacious plenty,
And yet seem cold, the time you may so hoodwink.

Why in that rawness left you wife and child,
Those precious motives, those strong knots of love,
Without leave-taking?

Sinful Macduff,
They were all struck for thee! naught that I am,
Not for their own demerits, but for mine,
Fell slaughter on their souls.

Be this the whetstone of your sword: let grief
Convert to anger; blunt not the heart, enrage it.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.
